<!-- Source: README.md -->

# @codenhub/icons

Zero-runtime icon system for the web. Write `ic-lucide-heart` in your markup and the icon arrives as a CSS mask — no imports, no components, no icon library in your bundle. One class, no JavaScript sitting around just to draw a heart.

`@codenhub/icons` ships 15 generated core icon families totalling over 36,000 icons, each with the license notices its artwork requires, so a project can adopt icons without spending an afternoon auditing licenses by hand. Two opt-in brand families add logos: `simple-icons`, over 3,000 in one brand color each, such as GitHub and npm, and `logos`, over 2,000 in full color, such as Google and Slack. Brand marks stay subject to their owners' trademark guidelines.

## Installation

```sh
pnpm add @codenhub/icons
```

## Usage

Icons reach a project through CSS. Pick the entry point that matches your pipeline; all of them understand the same classes.

### Tailwind CSS v4

One line. Every family except the brand families `simple-icons` and `logos` is resolvable, and Tailwind emits only the icons your markup used. To use a brand family, declare the plugin yourself with `families`, as in [Tailwind](docs/delivery/tailwind.md).

```css
@import "tailwindcss";
@import "@codenhub/icons/tw";
```

### Plain CSS, no build step

Import the base rules, then a stylesheet per family. Each family is complete, so nothing has to scan your markup — you trade file size for having zero build configuration.

```css
@import "@codenhub/icons";
@import "@codenhub/icons/lucide";
```

### Vite or PostCSS

The plugins scan your markup and generate only the rules it needs, which keeps the output small without Tailwind.

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import lucide from "@codenhub/icons/data/lucide";
import viteIcons from "@codenhub/icons/vite";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [viteIcons({ content: ["./src/**/*.{html,ts,tsx}"], defaultPrefix: "lucide", families: [lucide] })],
});
```

```css
@import "@codenhub/icons";
```

### No build tool

The `chi build` command reads your files and writes a stylesheet holding the base rules and only the icons they use, for a project that runs neither Tailwind CSS, Vite, nor PostCSS. Run it from a `package.json` script, or as `npx @codenhub/icons build`, as in [Build command](docs/delivery/cli.md).

```sh
npx @codenhub/icons build --content "app/views/**/*.erb" --output public/icons.css
```

### The markup

An icon is an element carrying an icon class — an `<i>`, or `.ic` on any element you own.

```html
<!-- standalone -->
<i class="ic-lucide-heart" aria-hidden="true"></i>

<!-- icon beside a label: a real element inside the control -->
<button class="btn"><i class="ic-lucide-check" aria-hidden="true"></i>Submit</button>

<!-- .ic, for a component that renders its own tag (CSS-based methods) -->
<span class="ic ic-lucide-search" aria-hidden="true"></span>

<!-- stroke width, for stroke-based families -->
<i class="ic-lucide-heart/1.5" aria-hidden="true"></i>

<!-- a size from the axis -->
<i class="ic-lucide-search ic-lg" aria-hidden="true"></i>

<i class="ic-lucide-loader-circle ic-anim-spin" aria-hidden="true"></i>
```

Size and color follow custom properties: set `--ic-size` and `--ic-color` on the icon or any ancestor. The `ic-xs`–`ic-xl` classes are shorthand that set `--ic-size` to a rem value; the default is `1em`. Icons paint in the text color, except brand icons, which arrive in their brand color until `--ic-color` says otherwise: `:root { --ic-color: currentColor; }` makes every icon monochrome. There is no `::before`, `::after`, or form-control form — for a `background-image` icon, resolve the `url()` with `getIconMaskUrl` / `getIconCssProps`.

## Requirements

| Requirement  | Details                                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Node.js      | 26 or newer, for the build-time plugins, helpers, and `chi build`.                                                                                           |
| CSS imports  | Consumer tooling must resolve package CSS imports.                                                                                                           |
| Browsers     | Must support CSS `mask-image`, which every method uses except inline SVG mode. Animated masks have been tested in Chromium; Firefox and Safari are untested. |
| Tailwind CSS | Version 4 or newer, and only for the `/tw` and `/tailwind` entry points.                                                                                     |
| Optional     | `vite` >= 5.0.0 for the Vite plugin, `postcss` >= 8.0.0 for the PostCSS plugin.                                                                              |

## Notes

- An icon is named `prefix:name`, written `ic-prefix-name` in a class, as in `ic-material-symbols-rounded-home`.
- The package names no default family, because nobody agrees on whether `close` is `x` or `times`. An unqualified `ic-heart` resolves only where you said what it means: through `defaultPrefix` in the Vite and PostCSS plugins, through `default:` in the Tailwind plugin, or, in the plugin-free path, through the last family stylesheet you imported that defines it. A family that has no icon by that name does not claim the bare selector, so an earlier family still answers to it, and the brand family stylesheets claim no bare names at all.
- Stroke width is a modifier on the icon class, `ic-lucide-heart/1.5`, and applies only to families drawn with strokes. It needs one of the plugins: a plugin-free stylesheet has no way to know which widths you want, so families there render at their authored width.
- An icon is an `<i>` (or `.ic` on any element, in the CSS-based methods). There is no `::before`, `::after`, or form-control form: an icon beside a label is a real `<i>` in the control, and a `background-image` icon comes from `getIconMaskUrl` / `getIconCssProps`.
- `anim` is reserved for [motion utilities](docs/concepts.md#motion); icon names cannot be `anim` or start with `anim-`, and the exact names `on-hover` and `trigger` are reserved too.
- `xs`, `sm`, `md`, `lg`, and `xl` are reserved (`ic-xs`–`ic-xl` are the size axis): no family may use one as a prefix or ship an icon by that name.
- Size follows `--ic-size`, default `1em`. The `ic-xs`–`ic-xl` classes each set it to a rem value (`0.75`, `0.875`, `1`, `1.25`, `1.5`) and nothing else, so they compose with a stroke modifier. An inlined `<svg>` from the renderer or `mode: "svg"` carries a `1em` box of its own and honours `--ic-size` through the base rules.
- The `/lucide` and other family stylesheets are large by construction — a whole family, because nothing is narrowing it, and `dist/css` totals about 39 MB across all 17. Import only the families you use, or use Tailwind or a plugin, which emit only what your markup asked for.
- `mode: "svg"` in the Vite plugin rewrites `<i class="ic-...">` tags into inline SVG and nothing else. A class on another element gets no icon in this mode; the plugin warns when it finds one.
- Animated artwork comes from `line-md` (1,222 icons) and `svg-spinners` (46 loading indicators). `ic-on-hover` shows static artwork at rest and plays it on hover with CSS alone. One-shot icons replay on every hover, rather than the first only, with the optional `@codenhub/icons/play` helper. Line MD masks stay static under reduced motion; inline SVG retains animation. See [Animated families](docs/concepts.md#animated-families) for setup and browser limits.
- Icon names are the upstream family's own: Material Symbols names keep their underscores, as in `ic-material-symbols-rounded-check_circle`.

## License

This package is licensed under the [Apache-2.0](LICENSE) license.

Its bundled, generated icon artwork comes from third parties, under ISC, MIT, Apache-2.0, and CC0 terms. See [NOTICE](NOTICE) for the full list. Each family stylesheet opens with its own notice, and the plugins emit the notices of the families a build actually used, so a consumer carries no separate obligation for them; see the documentation for the `attribution` options that control it. The brand families `simple-icons` and `logos` owe no license notice, but their marks are trademarks of their owners: using one is subject to that owner's brand guidelines, which no build setting satisfies. A third-party set adopted through `adoptIconifySet` is not covered — a consumer remains responsible for its license terms and attribution material.

<!-- Source: docs/index.md -->

# Icons through CSS, with no runtime

Getting icons onto a web page usually means one of three chores: copying SVG files by hand, wrapping every glyph in a framework component just to ship an icon, or dragging an entire icon library into your JavaScript bundle — and then spending a Friday afternoon tracking down MIT, ISC, and Apache-2.0 license notices. `@codenhub/icons` exists to skip all three.

Write a class such as `ic-lucide-heart` in your HTML and the build turns it into a CSS mask rule. There is no component layer, no icon library in your bundle, and nothing to import per icon — no JavaScript sitting around just to draw a heart. The package ships 15 generated core icon families totalling over 36,000 icons, each carrying the license notices its artwork requires, plus two opt-in brand families: over 3,000 one-color logos and over 2,000 full-color ones.

## Setup

### Installation

```sh
pnpm add @codenhub/icons
```

### Quick start

Icons reach a project through CSS. The shortest path with no build step is the base rules plus one family stylesheet — zero configuration required, provided you are fine loading the whole family:

```css
@import "@codenhub/icons";
@import "@codenhub/icons/lucide";
```

```html
<!-- standalone -->
<i class="ic-lucide-heart" aria-hidden="true"></i>

<!-- beside a label -->
<button><i class="ic-lucide-check" aria-hidden="true"></i>Submit</button>
```

An icon is an `<i>` carrying an icon class (or `.ic` on any element, in the CSS-based methods). Size and color follow custom properties: set `--ic-size` and `--ic-color` on the icon or any ancestor, or use the `ic-xs`–`ic-xl` size classes. Icons follow the text color, except brand icons, which arrive in their brand color; see [Color](docs/concepts.md#color).

Five delivery methods understand the same classes — plain CSS, Tailwind CSS v4, a Vite plugin, a PostCSS plugin, and the `chi build` command. The plugins and the command scan your markup and emit only the rules you used; the plain-CSS family stylesheets are complete and large by construction. See [Delivery methods](docs/delivery/index.md) to choose one, and [Frameworks](docs/frameworks/index.md) for framework-specific setup.

## Requirements

| Requirement  | Details                                                                         |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Node.js      | 26 or newer, for the build-time plugins, helpers, and `chi build`.              |
| CSS imports  | Consumer tooling must resolve package CSS imports.                              |
| Browsers     | Must support CSS `mask-image`, which every method uses except inline SVG mode.  |
| Tailwind CSS | Version 4 or newer, and only for the `/tw` and `/tailwind` entry points.        |
| Optional     | `vite` >= 5.0.0 for the Vite plugin, `postcss` >= 8.0.0 for the PostCSS plugin. |

## Reading path

Read these in order the first time. Each page builds on the last and points to the next one:

1. [Concepts](docs/concepts.md): families, finding icon names, name resolution, color, stroke width, size, motion, and accessibility — the shared model every delivery method builds on.
2. [Delivery methods](docs/delivery/index.md): the five ways icons reach your CSS and how to pick the one that fits your build.
3. [Frameworks](docs/frameworks/index.md): setup and framework-specific quirks for Astro, Next.js, and SvelteKit.
4. [JavaScript API](docs/javascript-api.md): the registry, renderers, runtime playback, and the third-party set adapter, for when you step outside a standard CSS build.
5. [Licensing](docs/licensing.md): attribution modes, obligation levels, trademark notes, and what each build owes.
6. [Troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md): an icon that renders as nothing, as a solid square, or at the wrong width.

When you need to look up a specific export or option, the [API reference](docs/reference/index.md) lists every export of `@codenhub/icons`, `/vite`, `/postcss`, and `/play`.

# How the icon system fits together

Every delivery method reads the same classes and follows the same rules. This page teaches that shared model once — from family names and color inheritance down to stroke width, size, and motion — so you can switch between plain CSS, Tailwind, Vite, or PostCSS without relearning how icons behave.

## Families

An icon family is a namespace of icons with its own prefix, geometry, and license, such as `lucide` or `material-symbols-rounded-fill`. Families are plain data modules generated from their upstream projects, which keeps artwork decoupled from any rendering framework:

```ts
import lucide from "@codenhub/icons/data/lucide";
import phosphorFill from "@codenhub/icons/data/phosphor-fill";
```

Available families:

| Prefix                                                           | Icons     | Style                       | License    |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | --------------------------- | ---------- |
| `line-md`                                                        | 1222      | animated, stroke-based      | MIT        |
| `svg-spinners`                                                   | 46        | animated loading indicators | MIT        |
| `lucide`                                                         | 2317      | outlined, stroke-based      | ISC        |
| `phosphor`                                                       | 1512      | outlined                    | MIT        |
| `phosphor-thin`, `phosphor-light`, `phosphor-bold`               | 1512 each | outlined, other weights     | MIT        |
| `phosphor-fill`                                                  | 1512      | filled                      | MIT        |
| `phosphor-duotone`                                               | 1512      | duotone                     | MIT        |
| `material-symbols-outlined`, `-rounded`, `-sharp`                | 3940 each | outlined                    | Apache-2.0 |
| `material-symbols-outlined-fill`, `-rounded-fill`, `-sharp-fill` | 3940 each | filled                      | Apache-2.0 |
| `simple-icons` (brand)                                           | 3255      | filled logos, brand-colored | CC0-1.0    |
| `logos` (brand)                                                  | 2016      | full-color logos            | CC0-1.0    |

Variants such as filled or duotone live in separate families rather than acting as toggles on one family. A class name stays a prefix and an icon name, with no extra variant syntax to guess.

`simple-icons` and `logos` are brand families, and they split the job: `simple-icons` draws each logo in one brand color, as in `ic-simple-icons-github` and `ic-simple-icons-npm`, while `logos` draws them in full color, as in `ic-logos-google-icon` and `ic-logos-slack-icon`, for brands that one color cannot show, such as Google's four-color G. Most brands appear in only one of the two, so they complement rather than duplicate each other.

Full-color logos naturally weigh more than single-color icons. With the build plugins, a project pays only for the logos it actually uses: about 2 KB of CSS for a typical logo, and under 8 KB for 95% of them. A handful of traced, highly detailed logos sit at the heavy end of the scale, from about 60 KB to 150 KB each: `lerna` (149 KB), `effector` (120 KB), `composer` (88 KB), `hugo` (85 KB), `tastejs` (69 KB), `matplotlib` (66 KB), `matplotlib-icon` (65 KB), and `chalk` (60 KB). Gzip or Brotli shrinks those figures several times over on the wire, and when weight still matters, prefer a lighter `-icon` variant or the brand's `simple-icons` entry if one exists. Brand families are opt-in everywhere — `@codenhub/icons/tw` never resolves them, and a declared `@plugin` resolves them only when its `families` option names them — and their marks remain trademarks of their owners. See [Licensing](docs/licensing.md#brand-families).

### Animated families

`line-md` provides 1,222 animated icons from Line MD 3.0.5 by Vjacheslav Trushkin, and `svg-spinners` provides 46 loading indicators by Utkarsh Verma, generated from the upstream SMIL artwork at commit `abfa05c49acf005b8b1e0ef8eb25a67a7057eb20`. Both are MIT-licensed core families, available through `@import "@codenhub/icons/tw"` by default, through the `@codenhub/icons/line-md` and `@codenhub/icons/svg-spinners` family stylesheets, or as `@codenhub/icons/data/line-md` and `@codenhub/icons/data/svg-spinners` for a configured plugin or registry.

```html
<i class="ic-line-md-heart/1.5" aria-hidden="true"></i>
<i class="ic-line-md-loading-loop" aria-hidden="true"></i>
<i class="ic-svg-spinners-90-ring" aria-hidden="true"></i>
```

The animations live inside the SVG artwork and run via SMIL. Line MD's `-loop` icons animate continuously, and its other icons draw in once. Without a [motion trigger](#motion), an icon plays the first time the page displays it. Chrome is verified; Firefox and Safari are untested, so do not infer animated-mask support from static-mask support.

Add `ic-on-hover` to show the static artwork at rest and play the animation while the trigger is hovered or has visible focus (`:focus-visible`), as described in [Motion](#motion):

```html
<button>
  <i class="ic-line-md-loading-loop ic-on-hover" aria-hidden="true"></i>
  Refresh
</button>
```

Looping icons play on every hover with CSS alone. A one-shot icon such as `ic-line-md-heart` plays on the first hover only with CSS alone, because browsers do not restart an animated image they have already painted once. To replay a one-shot icon on every hover, call [`bindIconPlayback`](docs/javascript-api.md#playing-icons-from-code) from `@codenhub/icons/play` once. Icons that have no static artwork keep their usual mask at rest.

CSS mode and inline SVG mode handle reduced motion and hover rest differently:

- **CSS-mask mode** (full family stylesheets, Tailwind, Vite CSS mode, and PostCSS, including stroke modifiers such as `/1.5`): under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, Line MD masks always paint the upstream static artwork, even during hover. Each icon carries its optional static artwork in `--ic-static-mask`, and the base rules pick it for reduced motion and hover rest. SVG Spinners have no static fallback, so provide an accessible loading label independently of their motion.
- **Inline SVG mode** (Vite's `mode: "svg"`, virtual modules, and `renderSvg`): keeps the animated `body`. Because CSS cannot stop a SMIL timeline, `ic-on-hover` cannot hold inline SVG artwork at rest, and those paths do not swap artwork for reduced motion. `playIcon` restarts an inline SVG, but skips the restart under reduced motion; it does not stop an already-running timeline. Choose CSS mode for the automatic swap, or read the resolved icon's `staticBody` before calling `renderSvg` when you need static inline artwork; `staticBody` shares the animated body's viewBox. `getIconMaskUrl` returns the animated artwork, while `getIconCssProps` also includes the static-mask property when available.

## Names

An icon is identified by `prefix:name`. Because CSS class names cannot contain colons, a class replaces the colon with a dash:

```html
<!-- lucide:heart -->
<i class="ic-lucide-heart"></i>

<!-- material-symbols-rounded:home -->
<i class="ic-material-symbols-rounded-home"></i>
```

When two loaded family prefixes share a start, the longest matching prefix wins, so `material-symbols-outlined` beats `material` when both are loaded.

An unqualified name such as `ic-heart` resolves against a configured default family, and against nothing at all when no default is set. The package picks no default family of its own and ships no semantic alias map, because nobody agrees on whether `close` should be `x` or `times`. So `ic-close` means whatever your chosen family calls `close`, and renders no icon if that family uses another name. Lucide calls that icon `x`, so under Lucide you write `ic-x`. In plain CSS, where multiple family stylesheets can be imported in sequence, a family stylesheet claims only the bare names it actually defines, so an earlier-imported family still answers for bare names the later family lacks.

Where the default family comes from depends on the delivery method:

| Method        | Default family                                                                                                                                |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Vite, PostCSS | The `defaultPrefix` option.                                                                                                                   |
| Tailwind      | The `default:` plugin option.                                                                                                                 |
| Plain CSS     | The last core family stylesheet imported. A brand family stylesheet claims no bare names, so importing one last leaves the default as it was. |

```ts
import { IconRegistry } from "@codenhub/icons";
import lucide from "@codenhub/icons/data/lucide";

const registry = new IconRegistry({ defaultPrefix: "lucide" });
registry.registerFamily(lucide);

registry.resolve("heart"); // lucide:heart
registry.resolve("close"); // undefined -- lucide calls it "x"
```

### Finding an icon's name

Icon names are always the upstream project's own, so browse the family's site and use the exact name shown there:

| Family                 | Browse at                                                                        | Example class                                   |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `line-md`              | [github.com/cyberalien/line-md](https://github.com/cyberalien/line-md)           | `ic-line-md-heart`, `ic-line-md-loading-loop`   |
| `svg-spinners`         | [github.com/n3r4zzurr0/svg-spinners](https://github.com/n3r4zzurr0/svg-spinners) | `ic-svg-spinners-90-ring`                       |
| `lucide`               | [lucide.dev/icons](https://lucide.dev/icons)                                     | `ic-lucide-circle-check`                        |
| `phosphor`, variants   | [phosphoricons.com](https://phosphoricons.com)                                   | `ic-phosphor-fill-check-circle`                 |
| `material-symbols-*`   | [fonts.google.com/icons](https://fonts.google.com/icons)                         | `ic-material-symbols-rounded-check_circle`      |
| `simple-icons` (brand) | [simpleicons.org](https://simpleicons.org)                                       | `ic-simple-icons-github`, `ic-simple-icons-npm` |
| `logos` (brand)        | [svgporn.com](https://svgporn.com)                                               | `ic-logos-google`, `ic-logos-google-icon`       |

Upstream naming quirks are kept as-is rather than normalized away:

- **Material Symbols** keeps Google's underscores: `check_circle`, not `check-circle`.
- **Simple Icons** uses the icon's slug, with any `_` written as `-`.
- **`logos`** uses the upstream file name, lowercased, with any `_` or `.` written as `-`: `socket.io` becomes `ic-logos-socket-io`. Some brands include both a full wordmark logo and a symbol with `-icon` appended, and some add `-dark` or `-alt` variants.

A misspelled name does not throw an error: the class resolves to nothing, so the element renders as a solid square when the base rules are loaded, or as nothing at all when they are missing. Check the name against the family when an icon disappears — or read the keys of the family module's `icons` object directly.

## Reserved names

Because utility classes live in the same `ic-*` namespace as icon classes, a few names are off-limits so your icons never collide with helpers:

- **`xs`, `sm`, `md`, `lg`, and `xl`** belong to the [size axis](#size) (`ic-xs` through `ic-xl`). No family may use one as a prefix. A core or extended family that ships an icon by that name fails generation; a brand family leaves that icon out and lists it in the family's attribution file.
- **`anim`, `on-hover`, and `trigger`** belong to the [motion utilities](#motion). A family cannot use `anim` as a prefix, and an icon named `anim` or starting with `anim-` is handled like a size name: it fails generation for a core or extended family and is left out of a brand family. The exact icon names `on-hover` and `trigger` are reserved the same way, while names that merely start with them — along with `animation` — stay available.
- **Stroke width** lives after a `/` on the icon class itself, so it claims no prefix at all.

## Markup

An icon is an HTML element carrying an icon class. Write an `<i>` — short, semantic-neutral, and the only element [inline SVG mode](docs/delivery/vite.md#inline-svg-mode) rewrites:

```html
<i class="ic-lucide-search" aria-hidden="true"></i>

<!-- stroke width, for stroke-based families only -->
<i class="ic-lucide-heart/1.5"></i>

<!-- a size from the axis -->
<i class="ic-lucide-search ic-lg"></i>
```

In the CSS-based methods, the same class also works on any element if you add `.ic`, which helps when a framework component insists on rendering its own tag:

```html
<span class="ic ic-lucide-search" aria-hidden="true"></span>
```

There is no `::before`, `::after`, or form-control form. An icon next to a label is a real `<i>` inside the button or link, so it lines up with flex or grid gaps and behaves the same across every delivery method. When you truly need a `background-image` icon — such as a custom control or an input affix — resolve its `url()` with [`getIconMaskUrl` or `getIconCssProps`](docs/javascript-api.md) and place it yourself.

Size and color follow CSS custom properties set on the icon or any ancestor:

```css
.toolbar {
  --ic-size: 1.25rem;
  --ic-color: var(--color-accent);
}
```

See [Size](#size) and [Color](#color).

## Color

An icon paints in the first source that applies, in this order:

1. `--ic-color`, set on the icon itself or inherited from any ancestor.
2. The icon's own artwork, for a full-color `logos` icon: `ic-logos-google-icon` keeps all four of Google's colors and its gradients.
3. The icon's own color, for `simple-icons`: `ic-simple-icons-github` uses GitHub's `#181717`, and `ic-simple-icons-npm` uses npm's `#cb3837`.
4. `currentColor`, matching the surrounding text color.

In short, core icons follow your text color automatically, while brand icons show up in their own brand colors until you tell them otherwise. Setting `--ic-color` overrides brand colors at whatever scope you set it; note that on a full-color logo, `--ic-color` turns the icon into a monochrome silhouette of its outline, so contrasting details inside the mark — such as the `31` on Google Calendar's icon — fill in solid:

```css
/* every icon on the page, brand icons included, in the text color */
:root {
  --ic-color: currentColor;
}

/* every icon in the toolbar */
.toolbar {
  --ic-color: var(--color-accent);
}

/* brand icons only, back to monochrome */
[class*="ic-simple-icons-"],
[class*="ic-logos-"] {
  --ic-color: currentColor;
}
```

```html
<!-- one icon -->
<i class="ic-simple-icons-npm" style="--ic-color: white" aria-hidden="true"></i>
```

To restore brand colors inside a subtree that sets `--ic-color`, reset the property on those icons with `--ic-color: initial`.

Some brand colors are near-black — GitHub, X, and Vercel among them — and vanish quietly on a dark background. Override those in your dark theme:

```css
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  .ic-simple-icons-github,
  .ic-simple-icons-x {
    --ic-color: white;
  }
}
```

With a custom class `prefix`, every custom property name matches: `--ux-color` under `prefix: "ux"`. Plain CSS `color` alone does not recolor a brand icon, because its own brand color sits ahead of `currentColor`; set `--ic-color` instead, or `--<prefix>-color` under a custom prefix. All of this works the same across every CSS delivery method and in [inline SVG mode](docs/delivery/vite.md#inline-svg-mode), where the brand colors travel inside the `<svg>` itself. One exception applies there: under a Content Security Policy that blocks `style` attributes, an inlined brand icon keeps its brand colors, but `--ic-color` (or `--<prefix>-color`) can no longer override them.

## Accessibility

An icon element has no text content, so assistive technology announces nothing for it, or an unhelpful guess. Mark each icon according to its role:

```html
<!-- decorative, beside a visible label: hide it -->
<button><i class="ic-lucide-trash" aria-hidden="true"></i>Delete</button>

<!-- the only content of a control: label the control, hide the icon -->
<button aria-label="Delete"><i class="ic-lucide-trash" aria-hidden="true"></i></button>

<!-- meaningful on its own, outside a control: give it a role and a name -->
<i class="ic-lucide-triangle-alert" role="img" aria-label="Warning"></i>
```

In [inline SVG mode](docs/delivery/vite.md#inline-svg-mode), attributes you place on the `<i>` carry over to the `<svg>` that replaces it.

## Stroke width

Stroke width is a modifier written right onto the icon class, and only families drawn with strokes answer to it. Of the bundled families, Lucide and Line MD support it; the other families ignore it:

```html
<!-- a thinner stroke -->
<i class="ic-lucide-heart/1.5"></i>

<!-- a heavier stroke -->
<i class="ic-lucide-heart/3"></i>
```

The width is baked directly into the SVG artwork the rule carries, so it cannot be applied as a separate class on top. `ic-heart` and `ic-heart/1.5` are two distinct icons as far as CSS is concerned, not one icon with a toggle. Because one class produces one rule, your stylesheet only pays for the stroke widths you actually wrote.

That is also why the modifier requires a build step: Vite, PostCSS, and Tailwind all scan your markup and generate the requested widths on demand, whereas the plugin-free family stylesheets render every icon at its authored width.

## Size

The default icon size is `1em`, matching the font size around it. Set `--ic-size` on the icon or any ancestor to resize it, or add a class from the size axis:

| Class   | `--ic-size` |
| ------- | ----------- |
| `ic-xs` | `0.75rem`   |
| `ic-sm` | `0.875rem`  |
| `ic-md` | `1rem`      |
| `ic-lg` | `1.25rem`   |
| `ic-xl` | `1.5rem`    |

```html
<i class="ic-lucide-search ic-lg"></i>
```

Each size class does one thing — set `--ic-size` to a rem value — so it composes cleanly with stroke modifiers and works regardless of which element it lands on. Unlike stroke width, size is not baked into the artwork, so the axis ships with the base rules and works in every delivery method, including [inline SVG mode](docs/delivery/vite.md#inline-svg-mode) as long as `@import "@codenhub/icons"` is present. Using `.ic` on a non-`<i>` element remains CSS-based methods only, as noted in [Markup](#markup).

Because these five classes are always emitted, `xs`, `sm`, `md`, `lg`, and `xl` are [reserved](#reserved-names): no family can ship an icon or take a prefix by those names.

## Motion

Icons move in two ways: motion classes animate the entire glyph for any icon in any family, while [animated families](#animated-families) animate their own artwork with no motion class needed. Three controls govern both:

| Question      | Control                                                                           | Default                                    |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| What moves    | an `ic-anim-*` class, or an animated family's icon                                | nothing                                    |
| When it plays | always, `ic-on-hover`, or [`playIcon`](docs/javascript-api.md#playing-icons-from-code) | always                                     |
| How often     | `--ic-anim-iterations`                                                            | forever; once per hover with `ic-on-hover` |

Five whole-glyph motion classes ship with the base styles:

| Class            | Motion                                         | Default duration |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| `ic-anim-spin`   | A full turn at a constant speed                | `1s`             |
| `ic-anim-pulse`  | Opacity fades between 1 and 0.55               | `2s`             |
| `ic-anim-beat`   | Two small heartbeats, up to 1.1 times its size | `1s`             |
| `ic-anim-bounce` | A vertical bounce, 15% of the icon's height    | `1s`             |
| `ic-anim-wiggle` | Rotation back and forth by 6 degrees           | `1s`             |

`ic-anim-spin` uses linear timing; the other four ease in and out. Set `--ic-anim-duration` on the icon or an ancestor to change the cycle length. Use at most one motion class per element: it replaces the element's CSS `animation`, and the transform-based motions also replace its `transform` while running.

**Always.** With no trigger class, the motion runs for as long as the class is on the element. Toggle `ic-anim-spin` on a reload icon while a request is in flight and drop it when the request finishes:

```html
<i class="ic-lucide-loader-circle ic-anim-spin" aria-hidden="true"></i>
```

**On hover.** `ic-on-hover` plays the motion while its trigger is hovered or has `:focus-visible`, and rests otherwise. The trigger can be the icon itself, its parent element, or any ancestor carrying `ic-trigger` — handy for cards or buttons where the icon sits inside a wrapper. Each hover restarts from the beginning and plays once by default:

```html
<button>
  <i class="ic-lucide-refresh-cw ic-anim-spin ic-on-hover" aria-hidden="true"></i>
  Reload
</button>

<a class="card ic-trigger" href="/inbox">
  <span class="card-icon"><i class="ic-lucide-bell ic-anim-wiggle ic-on-hover" aria-hidden="true"></i></span>
  Notifications
</a>
```

**How often.** `--ic-anim-iterations` sets the repeat count: any number, or `infinite`. Set `--ic-anim-iterations: infinite` when an icon should keep moving for the whole hover, such as a fan. Because it inherits, one rule on a toolbar sets the count for every icon inside it. Animated artwork follows its own authored timeline and ignores `--ic-anim-iterations`: Line MD `-loop` icons repeat, and the rest play once.

**From code.** For feedback tied to an event — a copy icon flashing on success, or a like icon popping on click — call `playIcon(element)` from the opt-in [`@codenhub/icons/play`](docs/javascript-api.md#playing-icons-from-code) entry point. It restarts glyph motion and animated artwork alike.

The base import, `@import "@codenhub/icons"`, includes the keyframes and motion classes, so they work with plain CSS family stylesheets, Vite, PostCSS, and inline SVG mode. Tailwind also registers them as utilities, keeping variants such as `group-hover:ic-anim-spin` available. With a custom class `prefix`, every class, custom property, and keyframe name shifts together: `ux-anim-spin`, `ux-on-hover`, `ux-trigger`, `--ux-anim-duration`, and `--ux-anim-iterations` under `prefix: "ux"`.

When the user's device requests reduced motion, motion classes stop, Line MD shows its static artwork even while hovered, and `playIcon` does nothing. SVG Spinners keep moving, because they have no static artwork. Keep loading or status information available in text; movement should never be the only way to understand a state.

Motion classes move the whole icon element. In CSS-mask mode, the artwork is an image, so CSS cannot reach inside it to target or animate individual paths. `ic-on-hover` relies on complex `:not()` selectors and `:focus-visible`, which work together in Chrome 88+, Firefox 85+, and Safari 15.4+. Motion was verified in Chrome; Firefox and Safari are untested.

## Next

Read [Delivery methods](docs/delivery/index.md) to pick how icon classes become CSS in your build — plain CSS, Tailwind CSS v4, Vite, or PostCSS.

<!-- Source: docs/delivery/index.md -->

# How icons reach your CSS

Every delivery method understands the exact same icon classes, and every CSS method produces the same mask rules for them. The one exception is the Vite plugin's [inline SVG mode](docs/delivery/vite.md#inline-svg-mode), which rewrites `<i>` tags into `<svg>` elements and emits no mask rules at all. Among the CSS methods, what changes between them is where those per-icon rules come from: either a prebuilt stylesheet containing every icon in a family, or a plugin or command that scans your markup and generates only the icons you wrote. This page compares all five options so you can pick the one that fits your build.

## Entry points

| Entry                      | For                         | What it delivers                                                                                                                                   |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@codenhub/icons`          | Every method                | The base `.ic` rules, about 2 KB. Never rewritten by a plugin.                                                                                     |
| `@codenhub/icons/tw`       | Tailwind CSS v4             | Base rules plus the plugin. Every non-brand family resolvable, only used icons emitted. Brand families need `@plugin` with `families` naming them. |
| `@codenhub/icons/tailwind` | Tailwind CSS v4, configured | The plugin on its own, so `@plugin` can carry options.                                                                                             |
| `@codenhub/icons/<family>` | Plain CSS, no build step    | One complete family, every icon written out.                                                                                                       |
| `@codenhub/icons/vite`     | Vite                        | Scans your markup and generates only the rules it needs.                                                                                           |
| `@codenhub/icons/postcss`  | PostCSS                     | The same, for a PostCSS pipeline.                                                                                                                  |
| `chi build`                | A build with none of these  | A command that reads your files and writes a stylesheet of the base rules and only the icons they use.                                             |

`@import "@codenhub/icons"` means one thing everywhere: the base rules that icon classes build on. No plugin rewrites it, and no plugin strips it out. The only moving part is which mechanism generates the per-icon mask rules beside it.

## Choosing one

| If your project…                                           | Use                          |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Already uses Tailwind CSS v4                               | [Tailwind](docs/delivery/tailwind.md)      |
| Builds with Vite (or a Vite-based framework)               | [Vite plugin](docs/delivery/vite.md)       |
| Runs a PostCSS pipeline but not Vite (Next.js, others)     | [PostCSS plugin](docs/delivery/postcss.md) |
| Runs none of these, but can run a command before deploying | [Build command](docs/delivery/cli.md)      |
| Has no build step, or you want the simplest possible setup | [Plain CSS](docs/delivery/plain-css.md)    |

The plugins and the build command keep CSS output small with no manual pruning: a project using three icons ships about 10 KB of CSS. Plain-CSS family stylesheets take the opposite trade — zero build setup in exchange for shipping every icon in the family, where Lucide alone is about 1.3 MB and all 17 families together reach about 39 MB.

One capability also depends on a build step: the `ic-lucide-heart/1.5` stroke-width modifier needs Tailwind, Vite, PostCSS, or the build command, because plain CSS stylesheets render stroke families at their authored width. See [Concepts](docs/concepts.md) for the shared model.

## Next

Read the guide for the method you picked — starting with [Plain CSS](docs/delivery/plain-css.md) if you want zero setup — or jump straight to [Frameworks](docs/frameworks/index.md) for Astro, Next.js, and SvelteKit wiring.

<!-- Source: docs/delivery/plain-css.md -->

# Plain CSS, no build step

Plain CSS is the zero-configuration route: import the base rules, then import one prebuilt stylesheet for each family you want. Every family stylesheet already holds its full catalog, so nothing needs to scan your markup.

```css
@import "@codenhub/icons";
@import "@codenhub/icons/phosphor-fill";
@import "@codenhub/icons/lucide";
```

Each rule carries two selectors sharing one copy of the artwork: the qualified `ic-lucide-heart` and the bare `ic-heart`. That is how plain CSS gets a default family with no plugin config to hold it — by standard CSS cascade order, the last family you import wins every bare name it defines. Above, `ic-heart` is Lucide's.

The brand families are the polite exception. `@codenhub/icons/simple-icons` and `@codenhub/icons/logos` emit only qualified names such as `ic-logos-google`, so importing one at the end never hijacks `ic-x` or `ic-play`.

## Cost

Because nothing scans your markup to prune unused icons, family stylesheets ship every glyph up front: Lucide is about 1.3 MB, Material Symbols Rounded about 3.9 MB, the full-color `logos` about 6.5 MB, Line MD about 3.0 MB including its static reduced-motion artwork, and all 17 families together reach about 39 MB. You control the budget by importing only the families you actually use. If that still feels heavy for three buttons and a sidebar, switch to Tailwind, Vite, or PostCSS so only the icons you wrote land in the output.

Line MD carries static artwork for reduced motion and for `ic-on-hover` at rest. Add `ic-on-hover` to play the artwork on hover with CSS alone; replaying one-shot artwork on every hover, rather than only the first, needs the optional `@codenhub/icons/play` helper. SVG Spinners retain loading animation. See [Animated families](docs/concepts.md#animated-families) for one-shot timing and browser limits.

## Limitations

Stroke width does not work in plain CSS. The width is baked into each rule's artwork, and a static stylesheet with no build step behind it has no way to know which stroke widths your templates asked for, so stroke families render at their authored width.

## See also

- [Delivery methods](docs/delivery/index.md) — how the methods compare.
- [Tailwind CSS](docs/delivery/tailwind.md) — the next delivery method, if you want on-demand emission with one import.
- [Frameworks](docs/frameworks/index.md) — framework-specific wiring once you have picked a delivery method.
- [Concepts](docs/concepts.md) — name resolution and the markup forms.

<!-- Source: docs/delivery/tailwind.md -->

# Tailwind CSS v4

If your project already runs Tailwind CSS v4, adding icons takes one import — zero plugin config required, and Tailwind emits only the icons your templates actually wrote:

```css
@import "tailwindcss";
@import "@codenhub/icons/tw";
```

Every family the package ships is resolvable out of the box except the brand families `simple-icons` and `logos`, which require declaring `@plugin` yourself with `families` (below). Loading the families costs about 150–190 ms and 112 MB once per build, both brand families included, against about 35 ms and 53 MB for a single family; a project using three icons ends up with about 10 KB of CSS.

## Configuring the plugin

When you want to restrict families, set a default prefix, change the class prefix, or opt into brand icons, declare `@plugin "@codenhub/icons/tailwind"` directly instead of importing `/tw` (which already declares it with no options):

```css
@import "tailwindcss";
@import "@codenhub/icons";
@plugin "@codenhub/icons/tailwind" {
  families: lucide, phosphor-fill;
  default: lucide;
  stroke-width: 1.5;
}
```

| Option         | Purpose                                                               |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `families`     | Family prefixes to resolve against. Defaults to all but brand ones.   |
| `default`      | Family that unqualified names resolve against. There is no default.   |
| `prefix`       | Class prefix. Defaults to `ic`.                                       |
| `stroke-width` | Applied to stroke-based families that carry no modifier of their own. |
| `attribution`  | `auto` or `off`. See [Licensing](docs/licensing.md).                    |

Notice one honest quirk: narrowing `families` does not make the build faster or lighter in memory. Because a Tailwind plugin handler has to run synchronously — utilities registered after an `await` are quietly dropped — every family is already loaded before your options are read. What `families` controls is which names can resolve and which license notices your built CSS carries.

## Motion

Motion classes and `ic-on-hover` work as Tailwind utilities, matching [Motion](docs/concepts.md#motion): `ic-on-hover` plays the motion while the icon, its parent, or an `ic-trigger` ancestor is hovered or has visible focus (`:focus-visible`), once per hover unless `--ic-anim-iterations` says otherwise, and it controls animated artwork as well:

```html
<button>
  <i class="ic-lucide-refresh-cw ic-anim-spin ic-on-hover" aria-hidden="true"></i>
  Reload
</button>
```

Because motion classes are real Tailwind utilities, Tailwind's variants remain available for other triggers. A variant replaces `ic-on-hover` for glyph motion and repeats until the state ends:

```html
<button class="group">
  <i class="ic-lucide-loader-circle group-hover:ic-anim-spin" aria-hidden="true"></i>
  Refresh
</button>
<i class="ic-lucide-bell hover:ic-anim-wiggle" aria-hidden="true"></i>
```

When using variants, pair `group-focus-visible:ic-anim-spin` with `group-hover:ic-anim-spin` so keyboard users get the same cue; `ic-on-hover` handles visible focus automatically. Reduced-motion preferences disable animations even when a variant matches. Animated artwork has no variant form, so keep `ic-on-hover` beside the icon class for those. See [Motion](docs/concepts.md#motion) for all five classes, defaults, custom prefixes, and CSS-mask animation limits.

## Attribution

`@import "@codenhub/icons/tw"` inlines a static stylesheet, so it carries an ordinary `/*! … */` banner naming every family it resolves — a superset notice that is always safe. Declaring `@plugin` yourself narrows resolution, and there the notice travels as a `--ic-attribution-<family>` custom property on `:root` instead, emitted once per family the build actually used. See [Licensing](docs/licensing.md).

## See also

- [Delivery methods](docs/delivery/index.md) — how the methods compare.
- [Vite plugin](docs/delivery/vite.md) — the next delivery method, for Vite builds without Tailwind.
- [Frameworks](docs/frameworks/index.md) — framework-specific wiring once you have picked a delivery method.
- [Concepts](docs/concepts.md) — name resolution and stroke width.

<!-- Source: docs/delivery/vite.md -->

# Vite plugin

When your build runs on Vite without Tailwind, the Vite plugin scans your files and serves only the CSS mask rules your markup uses — or rewrites `<i class="ic-...">` tags straight into inline SVGs if you prefer no stylesheet per icon at all.

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import lucide from "@codenhub/icons/data/lucide";
import viteIcons from "@codenhub/icons/vite";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [viteIcons({ content: ["./src/**/*.{html,ts,tsx}"], defaultPrefix: "lucide", families: [lucide] })],
});
```

```css
@import "@codenhub/icons";
```

| Option          | Purpose                                                                                     |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `families`      | Families to resolve against. Nothing is bundled by default.                                 |
| `defaultPrefix` | Family an unqualified name resolves against. There is no default.                           |
| `content`       | Files and globs to scan, beyond what the build transforms.                                  |
| `prefix`        | Class prefix. Defaults to `ic`.                                                             |
| `strokeWidth`   | Default for stroke-based families whose classes carry no modifier.                          |
| `mode`          | `css` serves mask rules; `svg` replaces `<i class="ic-...">` with inline SVG at build time. |
| `attribution`   | `auto`, `file`, or `off`. See [Licensing](docs/licensing.md).                                 |
| `registry`      | A prepared `IconRegistry`, replacing `families`.                                            |

The generated stylesheet is served as `virtual:icons.css` and injected into every HTML entry point. `@import "@codenhub/icons";` is left alone — it resolves through the package's `style` export condition to the base `.ic` rules and means the same thing whether or not a plugin is in the pipeline. Keep it in your stylesheet; the plugin adds the per-icon rules around it rather than in place of it.

## Scanning

`content` accepts literal paths and glob patterns such as `src/**/*.{html,tsx}`, expanded when the scan runs. Relative paths resolve from Vite's [`root`](https://vite.dev/config/shared-options.html#root), matching how Vite resolves its own paths, so the same config works no matter which directory you launch the build from. `content` is additive: the plugin also scans every source file Vite transforms, so you only need `content` for files the bundler never sees — and for clean first paints in dev.

The transform-time scan reads every module Vite transforms, whatever its extension. A file Vite never transforms is seen only through `content`, and so is a class in a module transformed after the stylesheet was generated, which can happen where a framework imports the stylesheet itself, as Astro and SvelteKit do. See [Frameworks](docs/frameworks/index.md). Note that this applies only to stylesheet generation; [inline SVG mode](#inline-svg-mode) rewrites a separate set of file types.

In dev, Vite serves the HTML shell before transforming a single JavaScript module, so an icon class written only inside a component module is still a mystery when the page first loads. To avoid leaving it blank, dev serves the stylesheet as a module rather than inlining it, and the plugin invalidates that module whenever a transform reveals a new class — the icon arrives without a page reload. Listing your sources in `content` skips that catch-up round trip altogether because the files are read from disk up front.

In `css` mode, a production build with HTML entries writes the stylesheet as a CSS asset named after its content hash, `assets/codenhub-icons-[hash].css` by default, and links it from every HTML entry. Because a build transforms all modules before emitting HTML, that file already holds every class the build saw. A build without HTML entries, such as a library build, emits no stylesheet, and neither does [inline SVG mode](#inline-svg-mode). A linked stylesheet asset needs no nonce or hash in a Content Security Policy: `style-src 'self'` allows it when served from the page's origin. With a `base` on another origin, such as a CDN, the policy must allow that origin, as it already must for Vite's own CSS. Two alternatives were rejected:

- **An inline `<style>`**. A policy without `'unsafe-inline'`, a nonce, or a hash refuses it, so every icon would render blank in production while dev, which uses a same-origin module script, still works.
- **A `nonce` option on the plugin.** Vite's own [`html.cspNonce`](https://vite.dev/config/shared-options#html-cspnonce) already stamps a nonce on the tags in the built HTML, and a nonce needs a server that sends a fresh one per response, which a static host cannot do.

## Inline SVG mode

`mode: "svg"` skips stylesheet generation completely and rewrites `<i class="ic-...">` tags into inline `<svg>` elements at build time. It rewrites `<i>` tags and nothing else: an icon class on another element — or `.ic` on a `<span>` — renders nothing in this mode because there is no stylesheet to supply its mask. The plugin warns at build time when it finds an icon class on an element it will not rewrite, naming the class and the file.

Animated SVG artwork keeps its SMIL animation in this mode, including when reduced motion is requested: CSS cannot stop SMIL. The static Line MD fallback, and `ic-on-hover` holding artwork at rest, apply only in CSS mode; glyph motion classes work in both. The optional `@codenhub/icons/play` helper restarts an inline SVG with `setCurrentTime(0)`; it skips restarts under reduced motion but does not stop existing SMIL animation. See [Animated families](docs/concepts.md#animated-families) for timing and browser limits.

Switching an existing project from CSS mode takes more than flipping a config flag, because the element reaching the browser changes from `<i>` to `<svg>`. Check two details your old `<i>` handled quietly:

- **Size.** The rendered `<svg>` carries a `1em` box as a presentation attribute, so an icon renders at text size with no stylesheet at all. CSS still wins over that: keep `@import "@codenhub/icons"` in a stylesheet and the base rules size the inlined `<svg>` from `--ic-size` exactly as they size an `<i>`, so setting `--ic-size` on an ancestor and the `ic-xs`–`ic-xl` classes both work. Without that import an icon is fixed at `1em`.
- **`hidden`.** `[hidden] { display: none }` is a user-agent rule for HTML elements, and an inlined icon is in the SVG namespace, so the attribute no longer hides it. Script that toggles an icon needs an explicit `[hidden] { display: none }` rule, and a guard written as `instanceof HTMLElement` stops matching — an SVG element is not one.

One limitation is new to logos. About 400 `logos` icons draw with gradients, masks, or clip paths, which they reach by `id`. Each logo's ids are prefixed with its name, so two different logos never collide, but two copies of the same logo share them, and the browser draws both copies from the first. If that first copy is inside an element hidden with `display: none`, as in a collapsed mobile menu, every later copy renders blank (seen in Chromium). Keep a visible copy ahead of the hidden one, hide with `visibility: hidden` instead, or use CSS mode for a logo that appears more than once, since each mask image there is a document of its own. The same applies to `renderSvg` and [one module per icon](#one-module-per-icon).

Rewriting covers `.html`, `.js`, `.jsx`, `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.vue`, `.svelte`, and `.astro`. An `.astro` file is rewritten in both halves, its frontmatter escaped as JavaScript and its template left as markup; `.vue` and `.svelte` files split the same way, with the template read as markup and `<script>` as JavaScript. An icon written as a JSX element receives React's attribute names, such as `strokeWidth`, and a `style` object when the project uses `@vitejs/plugin-react` or `@vitejs/plugin-react-swc`; Solid, Preact, and Vue JSX receive the HTML names, which they pass straight to the DOM. `content` plays no part in `svg` mode because it feeds stylesheet generation, which this mode skips.

Write every icon class out in full as a literal string so the plugin can spot it: a class assembled at runtime, such as `` `ic-${name}` ``, is invisible at build time. In CSS mode that element simply misses a rule; in `svg` mode there is no stylesheet at all to fall back on, so the element renders nothing. Whenever the icon name comes from state or data at runtime, use [one module per icon](#one-module-per-icon) — it is the supported pattern and works in both modes.

## One module per icon

When an icon is chosen dynamically at runtime, import a virtual module for that icon instead of shipping a whole family:

```ts
const { svg } = await import("virtual:@codenhub/icons/lucide/heart");
element.innerHTML = svg;
```

The module exports the rendered markup as both `svg` and its default export, alongside the resolved icon object as `icon`. The `<svg>` carries the icon's qualified class (such as `ic-lucide-heart` under the configured `prefix`) just like inline SVG mode, so the base rules size and color it via `--ic-size`, `--ic-color`, and the `ic-xs`–`ic-xl` classes. It carries no `aria-hidden` attribute: add it yourself for a decorative icon, or give a meaningful icon `role="img"` and a label. Each import becomes its own module, letting the bundler code-split and tree-shake down to single icons. An unqualified path such as `virtual:@codenhub/icons/close` resolves through your configured default prefix like any other bare name, and an unknown icon fails the build loudly rather than shipping a blank element.

## See also

- [Delivery methods](docs/delivery/index.md) — how the methods compare.
- [PostCSS plugin](docs/delivery/postcss.md) — the next delivery method, for non-Vite PostCSS builds.
- [Frameworks](docs/frameworks/index.md) — Astro and SvelteKit build on this plugin.
- [JavaScript API](docs/javascript-api.md) — preparing a `registry` by hand.

<!-- Source: docs/delivery/postcss.md -->

# PostCSS plugin

For builds that run PostCSS without Vite or Tailwind — most often Next.js — the PostCSS plugin scans your stylesheets and `content` globs, then appends the base rules and just the mask rules your markup uses.

```ts
import lucide from "@codenhub/icons/data/lucide";
import postcssIcons from "@codenhub/icons/postcss";

postcssIcons({
  content: ["./src/**/*.html"],
  families: [lucide],
  defaultPrefix: "lucide",
  injectBase: true,
  attribution: "auto",
});
```

It shares the same `families`, `defaultPrefix`, `prefix`, and `strokeWidth` options as the [Vite plugin](docs/delivery/vite.md). Because PostCSS has no asset pipeline of its own, `attribution` accepts `auto` and `off` only, and there is no `mode: "svg"`.

| Option          | Purpose                                                            |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `content`       | Files and globs to scan for icon classes.                          |
| `families`      | Families to resolve against. Nothing is bundled by default.        |
| `defaultPrefix` | Family an unqualified name resolves against.                       |
| `injectBase`    | Whether to append the base `.ic` rules. Defaults to `true`.        |
| `prefix`        | Class prefix. Defaults to `ic`.                                    |
| `strokeWidth`   | Default for stroke-based families whose classes carry no modifier. |
| `attribution`   | `auto` or `off`. See [Licensing](docs/licensing.md).                 |
| `registry`      | A prepared `IconRegistry`, replacing `families`.                   |

## Scanning

Unlike the Vite plugin, this plugin has no visibility into the bundler's module graph. When it runs on a stylesheet, it sees only that stylesheet's own text and the files matched by `content` — nothing else. List globs covering everywhere your icon classes live (components, templates, HTML), or only classes written literally inside your CSS will resolve:

```ts
postcssIcons({
  content: ["./app/**/*.{tsx,jsx,mdx}", "./components/**/*.{tsx,jsx}"],
  families: [lucide],
  defaultPrefix: "lucide",
});
```

The plugin runs once for every stylesheet it processes, so attach it to a single global stylesheet rather than running it across every CSS module.

## See also

- [Delivery methods](docs/delivery/index.md) — how the methods compare.
- [Frameworks](docs/frameworks/index.md) — next on the reading path, covering Astro, Next.js, and SvelteKit.
- [Frameworks: Next.js](docs/frameworks/nextjs.md) — the main reason to reach for PostCSS over Vite.

<!-- Source: docs/delivery/cli.md -->

# Build command

For a project with no Tailwind CSS, Vite, or PostCSS, such as a Rails, Laravel, or Django app, or a static site, the `build` command reads your files, finds the icon classes they use, and writes a stylesheet holding only those icons. A page with three icons gets about 10 KB of CSS rather than a complete family stylesheet, where Lucide alone is about 1.3 MB, and the `ic-lucide-heart/1.5` stroke-width modifier works as it does with the plugins.

Run it from a `package.json` script, where the package's command is named `chi`:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build:icons": "chi build --content \"app/views/**/*.erb\" --output public/icons.css"
  }
}
```

Or run it once without a script:

```sh
npx @codenhub/icons build --content "app/views/**/*.erb" --output public/icons.css
```

Use `npx @codenhub/icons`, not `npx chi`: an unrelated package named `chi` exists on npm, and `npx chi` runs it wherever this package is not installed.

Then link the stylesheet it wrote. It already holds the base `.ic` rules, so nothing else is imported:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/icons.css" />
```

Run the command again whenever your files change which icons they use, before each deploy at the least. It writes the same rules the [PostCSS plugin](docs/delivery/postcss.md) appends for the same files and options, so a project can move between the two without its CSS changing.

## Options

| Flag                          | Purpose                                                                                     |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-c`, `--content <glob>`      | Files to read for icon classes. Required and repeatable.                                    |
| `-o`, `--output <file>`       | Stylesheet to write. Required. Parent folders are created.                                  |
| `--family <prefix>`           | A family to resolve icons from. Repeatable. Defaults to every family except the brand ones. |
| `--default-prefix <prefix>`   | Family a bare name, such as `ic-heart`, resolves against. Without it, none resolves.        |
| `--prefix <prefix>`           | Class prefix. Defaults to `ic`.                                                             |
| `--stroke-width <width>`      | Default for stroke-based families whose classes carry no modifier.                          |
| `--no-base`                   | Leave out the base `.ic` rules, for a page that loads them from `@codenhub/icons` already.  |
| `--attribution <auto \| off>` | `auto` writes the license notices as a comment at the top; `off` writes none. See below.    |
| `--help`, `--version`         | Print the usage or the package version.                                                     |

Each option is the PostCSS plugin's, with the same default, except `--family`. The plugin resolves no family until you pass one, while the command resolves every family except `simple-icons` and `logos`, the brand families, whose marks carry their owners' trademark terms. Name a brand family to use it, along with every other family you use, since naming one replaces the default:

```sh
npx @codenhub/icons build --content "templates/**/*.html" --output static/icons.css --family lucide --family simple-icons
```

`--content` reads globs as the PostCSS plugin does: relative to the folder you run the command in, with `**` for any number of folders and `{html,erb}` for either extension. A path that names an existing file is read as that file, even when its name holds a bracket, such as Next.js's `app/[id]/page.tsx`. Quote each glob, with `\"` inside a `package.json` script, so your shell does not expand it first.

Write every icon class out in full in a file the command reads: a class assembled at runtime, such as `` `ic-${name}` ``, is not in the files, so its icon gets no rule and no warning. When the name comes from data, list each class it can take in full in a file under `--content`.

## Attribution

With `--attribution auto`, the default, the stylesheet starts with a preserved comment carrying the license notice of each family it used. A minifier keeps it unless it is set to drop legal comments, as `legalComments: "none"` is, so keep legal comments in your minifier's configuration. With `off`, it carries none, and the command warns when a family it used requires a notice, so you can ship that notice another way. [Licensing](docs/licensing.md) explains what each family requires.

## Failures and warnings

The command stops, writes nothing, and prints one line starting `chi:` when the build would be wrong:

- **`--content "<glob>" matches no file in <folder>`.** Usually a typo, or the command running from another folder than your project root. A build from missing files would write a stylesheet without some icons, and the site would lose them silently.
- **A file it cannot read**, with Node.js's own message.
- **`unexpected argument "<file>"`.** Almost always a `--content` glob without quotes, which your shell expanded. Quote the glob.
- **`unknown family`, `unknown default prefix`**, listing the valid ones, and **an `--attribution` other than `auto` or `off`**, or **a `--stroke-width` that is not a positive number**.
- **A Node.js older than 26**, naming both versions.

A class that resolves to no icon, such as a misspelled `ic-lucide-hart`, is a warning, not a failure: the command lists every such class once and still writes the stylesheet. A word that only looks like a class, such as `ic-` text in a comment, would otherwise stop a build.

## What it does not do

- **Inline SVG and per-icon modules.** They change your source files or serve modules to a bundler. Use the [Vite plugin](docs/delivery/vite.md).
- **A custom registry or an adopted icon set.** These take JavaScript values. Use a plugin.
- **Watch mode, a configuration file, and minification.** Run the command from your own watcher or build script, and minify its output in your own pipeline if you minify CSS.

## See also

- [Delivery methods](docs/delivery/index.md) — how the methods compare.
- [PostCSS plugin](docs/delivery/postcss.md) — the same rules, from a PostCSS pipeline.
- [Frameworks](docs/frameworks/index.md) — next on the reading path.

<!-- Source: docs/frameworks/index.md -->

# Framework setup

Every framework consumes `@codenhub/icons` through one of the [delivery methods](docs/delivery/index.md). Most Vite-based frameworks work out of the box without a dedicated guide, while a few have build pipelines or template extensions with opinions of their own. This section covers the three worth calling out.

| Framework                           | Recommended method                              | Notes                                                                                           |
| ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Astro](docs/frameworks/astro.md)                   | Plain CSS or Tailwind v4; Vite plugin with care | `.astro` is not auto-scanned by the Vite plugin — pass `content`.                               |
| [Next.js](docs/frameworks/nextjs.md)                | Tailwind v4 or PostCSS plugin                   | No Vite pipeline, so the Vite plugin does not apply.                                            |
| [SvelteKit](docs/frameworks/sveltekit.md)           | Vite plugin                                     | `.svelte` is auto-scanned; the cleanest plugin story.                                           |
| Vue, SolidStart, Nuxt, Remix (Vite) | Vite plugin                                     | Follow [SvelteKit](docs/frameworks/sveltekit.md); `.vue` is auto-scanned like `.svelte`.                        |
| Any framework                       | Plain CSS                                       | [Plain-CSS](docs/delivery/plain-css.md) family imports work everywhere that resolves package CSS. |

If your framework is missing from the table and builds with Vite, follow the [SvelteKit](docs/frameworks/sveltekit.md) guide. If it builds with webpack or another PostCSS host, follow [Next.js](docs/frameworks/nextjs.md). And if you just want icons on screen with zero build plumbing, [plain CSS](docs/delivery/plain-css.md) works anywhere at the cost of larger stylesheets.

## Next

Pick the framework guide above that matches your stack — starting with [Astro](docs/frameworks/astro.md) — or continue to the [JavaScript API](docs/javascript-api.md) when you need programmatic control outside a framework build.

<!-- Source: docs/frameworks/astro.md -->

# Astro

Astro runs on Vite, so all four [delivery methods](docs/delivery/index.md) are on the table. Two of them work without any Astro-specific wiring at all; the Vite plugin takes two extra lines because Astro renders production HTML outside Vite's own HTML pipeline.

## Plain CSS (no configuration)

Import the base rules and a family stylesheet from a layout or global stylesheet:

```css
/* src/styles/icons.css */
@import "@codenhub/icons";
@import "@codenhub/icons/lucide";
```

```astro
---
import "../styles/icons.css";
---
<i class="ic-lucide-heart" aria-hidden="true"></i>
```

Astro resolves the package's CSS exports directly. This is the least-effort path — one CSS import and zero config — at the cost of stylesheet size and no stroke-width modifier. See [Plain CSS](docs/delivery/plain-css.md).

## Tailwind CSS v4 (no configuration)

With `@tailwindcss/vite` configured, add one import to your Tailwind entry:

```css
@import "tailwindcss";
@import "@codenhub/icons/tw";
```

Only the icons your markup uses are emitted. See [Tailwind CSS](docs/delivery/tailwind.md).

## Vite plugin

Add the plugin in `astro.config.mjs`:

```js
import lucide from "@codenhub/icons/data/lucide";
import icons from "@codenhub/icons/vite";
import { defineConfig } from "astro/config";

export default defineConfig({
  vite: {
    plugins: [
      icons({
        families: [lucide],
        defaultPrefix: "lucide",
        content: ["./src/**/*.{astro,md,mdx,html}"],
      }),
    ],
  },
});
```

Then import the generated stylesheet once, from a layout every page uses:

```astro
---
import "../styles/global.css"; // your stylesheet holding @import "@codenhub/icons"
import "virtual:icons.css";
---
```

The first line is whatever stylesheet already carries `@import "@codenhub/icons";`; the base rules can live in any stylesheet the page loads. The second line is required, and Astro-specific. Everywhere else, the Vite plugin injects the generated stylesheet into the HTML through Vite's `transformIndexHtml` hook. A production `astro build` renders pages through Astro's own pipeline rather than as Vite HTML entries, so `transformIndexHtml` never runs on them and this explicit import is what puts the mask rules on the page. Without it, the build succeeds, `@import "@codenhub/icons"` still supplies the base rules, and every icon renders as a solid square in its color.

Keep the `content` entry. The plugin also scans every module Vite transforms, `.astro` files included, but the stylesheet is generated when the layout imports it, and a build can reach that import before Vite has transformed every page and component. `content` is what guarantees each class written in `.astro`, `.md`, or `.mdx` is in it.

Check that every class you write resolves in a family you registered. An icon name the registry cannot find is left without a rule and renders as a solid square. CSS mode reports nothing when that happens — in any host, not only in Astro — so the build stays green and the gap is visible only on the page. Inline SVG mode does warn, naming the class and the file.

## Inline SVG mode

`mode: "svg"` works in Astro and rewrites `<i class="ic-...">` tags inside `.astro` files — in the template, in the frontmatter, and in `<script>` blocks, each escaped for its context. An icon tag written inside a _string_ in a template expression, such as `{cond ? '<i class="ic-x"></i>' : ''}`, is the one place it goes wrong: it is rewritten as markup, without escaping for the quotes around it, because telling it apart from markup such as `{cond && <i class="ic-x" />}` requires a parser. The inlined SVG can then end the string early. Move that tag to the frontmatter or a component instead. Everything above about delivering the mask stylesheet stops applying here: `svg` mode emits no per-icon rules, so neither `virtual:icons.css` nor `content` does anything, and a class on any element other than an `<i>` tag renders nothing because there is no stylesheet behind it.

Keep `@import "@codenhub/icons"` even so. An inlined `<svg>` renders at `1em` on its own, but that base stylesheet is what lets `--ic-size` and the `ic-xs`–`ic-xl` size classes reach it. See [Vite plugin § Inline SVG mode](docs/delivery/vite.md#inline-svg-mode).

`.md` and `.mdx` are not rewritten. An icon class written in one of those reaches the page as a bare `<i>` element with no mask rule behind it, so it renders as a solid square with the base rules loaded, or as nothing without them. Nothing reports it, either: the unresolved-class warning only covers the files this mode rewrites, so such a page builds green and ships broken icons.

There are two ways through this:

- **In `.mdx`**, wrap the icon in a component and render that component from your markdown: the component lives in an `.astro`, `.jsx`, or `.tsx` file, all of which are rewritten.
- **In plain `.md`**, which cannot import components, use CSS mode instead so `content` globs cover `.md` and `.mdx` files just like any other template.

## See also

- [Vite plugin](docs/delivery/vite.md) — full option reference and the scanning model.
- [Delivery methods](docs/delivery/index.md) — how the methods compare.
- [Next.js](docs/frameworks/nextjs.md) and [SvelteKit](docs/frameworks/sveltekit.md) — the other framework guides.
- [JavaScript API](docs/javascript-api.md) — next on the reading path, for programmatic CSS or SVG generation.

<!-- Source: docs/frameworks/nextjs.md -->

# Next.js

Next.js builds with webpack or Turbopack rather than Vite, so `@codenhub/icons/vite` sits this one out. The other three delivery methods all work as expected — and because all three produce plain CSS, the App Router, React Server Components, and streaming are completely unaffected.

## Tailwind CSS v4

If your Next.js app already runs Tailwind v4 through `@tailwindcss/postcss`, one import in your global stylesheet covers every family except the brand ones:

```css
/* app/globals.css */
@import "tailwindcss";
@import "@codenhub/icons/tw";
```

Only the icons your markup uses are emitted. `/tw` never resolves the brand families `simple-icons` and `logos`; to use one, declare the plugin with `families` naming it, as in [Tailwind CSS § Configuring the plugin](docs/delivery/tailwind.md#configuring-the-plugin).

## PostCSS plugin

Without Tailwind, register the PostCSS plugin in `postcss.config.mjs` and pass `content` globs covering every directory where icon classes live — PostCSS inspects only the stylesheet text and `content`, with no visibility into the module graph:

```js
import lucide from "@codenhub/icons/data/lucide";
import icons from "@codenhub/icons/postcss";

export default {
  plugins: [
    icons({
      families: [lucide],
      defaultPrefix: "lucide",
      content: ["./app/**/*.{tsx,jsx,mdx}", "./components/**/*.{tsx,jsx}"],
    }),
  ],
};
```

The plugin appends the base rules itself, since `injectBase` defaults to `true`, so `app/globals.css` needs no `@import "@codenhub/icons";` here; importing it too would ship the base rules twice. To import them yourself instead, set `injectBase: false`. See [PostCSS plugin](docs/delivery/postcss.md).

## Plain CSS

Zero config and no PostCSS plugin, trading stylesheet size for simplicity:

```css
/* app/globals.css */
@import "@codenhub/icons";
@import "@codenhub/icons/lucide";
```

See [Plain CSS](docs/delivery/plain-css.md).

## See also

- [Delivery methods](docs/delivery/index.md) — how the methods compare.
- [Concepts](docs/concepts.md) — name resolution and the markup forms.
- [SvelteKit](docs/frameworks/sveltekit.md) — the Vite-based counterpart, if you want to compare setups.
- [JavaScript API](docs/javascript-api.md) — next on the reading path, for programmatic CSS or SVG generation.

<!-- Source: docs/frameworks/sveltekit.md -->

# SvelteKit

SvelteKit builds on Vite, and the Vite plugin scans every `.svelte` module Vite transforms. The one extra step is the same one Astro needs: SvelteKit renders pages itself rather than as Vite HTML entries, so the generated stylesheet has to be imported by hand.

## Vite plugin

Add the plugin in `vite.config.ts` alongside `sveltekit()`:

```ts
import { sveltekit } from "@sveltejs/kit/vite";
import lucide from "@codenhub/icons/data/lucide";
import icons from "@codenhub/icons/vite";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    sveltekit(),
    icons({
      families: [lucide],
      defaultPrefix: "lucide",
      content: ["./src/**/*.{svelte,html}"],
    }),
  ],
});
```

```css
/* src/app.css */
@import "@codenhub/icons";
```

Then import both stylesheets from the root layout, so every page loads them:

```svelte
<!-- src/routes/+layout.svelte -->
<script>
  import "../app.css";
  import "virtual:icons.css";

  let { children } = $props();
</script>

{@render children()}
```

The plugin injects its stylesheet through Vite's `transformIndexHtml` hook, which SvelteKit never runs on its pages, so the `virtual:icons.css` import is what puts the mask rules on the page. Without it, the base rules still apply and every icon renders as a solid square in its color.

Keep the `content` entry. The stylesheet is generated when the layout imports it, and a build can reach that import before Vite has transformed every component, so `content` is what guarantees each class is in it. It also keeps the first paint right in dev. `mode: "svg"` also works directly on `.svelte` files.

## Other methods

[Tailwind CSS v4](docs/delivery/tailwind.md) and [plain CSS](docs/delivery/plain-css.md) work in SvelteKit the same way they do everywhere else. A Vite single-page app with an `index.html`, such as one built with Vue or Solid, gets the stylesheet injected and needs no layout import; a framework that renders its own HTML, such as Nuxt or SolidStart, needs the import as SvelteKit does.

## See also

- [Vite plugin](docs/delivery/vite.md) — full option reference and the scanning model.
- [Delivery methods](docs/delivery/index.md) — how the methods compare.
